# Single Buy/Sell Profit — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/sliding-window/best-trade.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Sliding Window** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock/)

Given prices where prices[i] is a stock's price on day i, pick one day to buy and a later day to sell so profit is maximised. Return the profit, or 0 if no profitable trade exists.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= prices.length <= 10^5
- 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4
- the sell day must come after the buy day
- no profitable pair means a profit of 0, not a negative number

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]` | `5` | Buy at 1, sell at 6. |
| `prices = [5, 4, 3]` | `0` | Prices only fall — don't trade. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. For each sell day, the best buy day is simply the cheapest price seen so far.
2. One pass: carry the running minimum and the running best profit.
3. Selling before buying is impossible by construction — the minimum you compare against always comes from earlier days.

</details>

---

## 1. Brute force

Try every buy/sell day pair with the sell strictly later.

```python
def max_profit(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(prices)):
            best = max(best, prices[j] - prices[i])
    return best
```

**O(n²) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < prices.length; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < prices.length; j++) {
            best = Math.max(best, prices[j] - prices[i]);
        }
    }
    return best;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int maxProfit(const vector<int>& prices) {
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)prices.size(); i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < (int)prices.size(); j++) {
            best = max(best, prices[j] - prices[i]);
        }
    }
    return best;
}
```

</details>

## 2. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Every buy/sell pair asks the same question over and over. Walking once while remembering the cheapest day so far answers it with two numbers and no nested loop.

Scan left to right holding two numbers: the lowest price seen so far and the best profit so far. Each day, profit-if-sold-today is price minus that minimum; update both trackers. This is a shrunk sliding window: the left edge is always the historical minimum.

```python
def max_profit(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
    int lowest = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    int best = 0;
    for (int p : prices) {
        lowest = Math.min(lowest, p);
        best = Math.max(best, p - lowest);
    }
    return best;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int maxProfit(const vector<int>& prices) {
    int lowest = INT_MAX;
    int best = 0;
    for (int p : prices) {
        if (p < lowest) lowest = p;
        int profit = p - lowest;
        if (profit > best) best = profit;
    }
    return best;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brute force | O(n²) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(1) space | Every buy/sell pair asks the same question over and over. Walking once while remembering the cheapest day so far answers it with two numbers and no nested loop. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def max_profit_brute_force(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(prices)):
            best = max(best, prices[j] - prices[i])
    return best


def max_profit_the_one_to_remember(prices: list[int]) -> int:
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

APPROACHES = [
    max_profit_brute_force,
    max_profit_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# the minimum arriving AFTER a higher price — [7,1,5,3,6,4]; a falling series trades nothing
CASES = [
    lambda: ([7,1,5,3,6,4],),
    lambda: ([7,6,4,3,1],),
    lambda: ([2],),
    lambda: ([1,2],),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<32} -> {answers}")
```
